strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated core idea: the paper identifies a genuine trade-off in AR visual generation between fixed raster-scan order (good sampling performance, poor editing flexibility) and random permutation (flexible order, degraded performance), and proposes uniform spanning trees as a structured middle ground that preserves prior knowledge (locality, center bias) while retaining order flexibility.

The method is elegant and requires only minimal architectural changes (additional positional embeddings for the next-token position) on top of a standard decoder-only causal AR Transformer, which supports the authors' claim of a low-cost, broadly adoptable building block.

The entropy analyses (Figures 3 and 4) provide useful intuition: prediction entropy increases with distance from the prefix and toward the image center, empirically justifying the use of locality and corner-rooted spanning trees.

The rejection-sampling postfix-completion algorithm (Algorithm 1) is a practical contribution, and the ablation in Table 3 showing BFS dominates DFS (fewer trials to accept, fewer failures) is a concrete and convincing design justification.

Ablation studies are thorough and informative: Table 2 isolates the effect of order randomization strategy and shows that spanning-tree orderings consistently outperform random permutation and match raster-scan without annealing tricks, and the supplementary conditional-entropy analysis supports the uniformity argument.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: hyperparameters, tokenizer (MaskGIT-VQGAN), optimizer, schedules, and CFG settings are reported in the supplementary, and code is stated to be available.
The inpainting comparison (Figure 6, Figure 7) provides both quantitative and qualitative evidence that STAR enables out-of-order postfix completion that raster-scan AR models cannot achieve.
weaknesses: The headline class-conditional generation results do not surpass the strongest AR baseline (RAR). At matched scales STAR is consistently slightly worse (e.g., STAR-B FID 2.24 vs RAR-B 1.95; STAR-XXL 1.55 vs RAR-XXL 1.48), so the practical value proposition rests almost entirely on editing flexibility rather than improved generation, which weakens the 'without sacrificing performance' framing.

The editing capability—arguably the main motivation—is evaluated only on inpainting with a single masking strategy and a single baseline (RAR). Broader editing tasks (object insertion/removal, arbitrary mask shapes, user-driven partial completion) are not tested, so the generality of the flexibility claim is under-supported.

Evaluation is limited in scope: only ImageNet-1k at 256×256, class-conditional generation. There is no text-to-image, higher-resolution, or multimodal evaluation, even though the paper motivates STAR partly through compatibility with early-fusion multimodal models.

The inpainting comparison may be somewhat favorable to STAR by construction: RAR is a raster-scan model that was not designed for out-of-order postfix completion, so demonstrating superiority over RAR in this setting is a relatively weak test of the method's actual advantage; comparisons against masked-generation or bidirectional-context baselines more suited to this task would strengthen the case.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing order-randomization work (RandAR, RAR, MAR). The core mechanism—providing the position of the next token to be predicted via additional positional embeddings—is closely related to prior approaches; the specific choice of uniform spanning trees is a refinement rather than a fundamentally new capability.

The theoretical argument that the number of spanning trees grows as exp(N·z_G) with z_G≈1.166 (a smaller sample space than N!) is interesting but its practical consequence is unclear: the model is trained only on BFS traversals of spanning trees, so the claim of 'sufficiently covering' the useful order space is asserted rather than quantitatively demonstrated (e.g., coverage of raster-scan-like orders, or how often favorable orders are visited).

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports—e.g., the abstract's 'maintaining sampling performance without any significant changes to the model architecture widely adopted in the language AR modeling' glosses over the fact that generation performance is not actually better than raster-scan or RAR.

strengths: Proposes STAR, a simple and effective sequence-order randomization strategy for autoregressive visual generation based on BFS traversal of uniform spanning trees; the design preserves prefix connectivity while reflecting image priors such as center bias and locality, and enables flexible postfix completion for editing.

Provides useful empirical motivation via entropy analyses (Figures 3-4) showing that random-permutation AR models still exhibit center bias and locality effects, and validates the core design choices with ablations on order randomization, traversal strategy, and rejection sampling.

Demonstrates strong class-conditional generation on ImageNet 256x256: STAR is comparable to RAR and outperforms RandAR, with notably higher Inception Score at several scales; inpainting results across masking ratios (Figure 6) are substantially better than RAR.

The method requires minimal changes to a standard decoder-only AR Transformer, mostly additional positional embeddings; Algorithm 1 and the BFS/DFS comparison (Table 3) give a clear and practical recipe for postfix completion.

Reproducibility is generally good: code is promised, hyperparameters and architecture details are provided, and experiments follow established evaluation protocols on ImageNet with FID, IS, Precision, and Recall.
weaknesses: The generation FID does not surpass the raster-scan RAR baseline at any model scale (e.g., STAR-XXL 1.55 vs. RAR-XXL 1.48), so the 'sampling performance' claim is closer to parity or a trade-off with IS than a clear improvement.

The prior-knowledge argument is largely heuristic and empirical; the entropy analysis is performed on random-permutation models rather than directly on STAR, and there is no formal guarantee that uniform spanning trees optimally encode center bias or locality.

Editing evaluation is limited to inpainting with random connected masks on ImageNet; other editing tasks such as outpainting, text-guided editing, or object removal are not evaluated, and the method assumes connected partial observations and masks that do not cover every corner, which may limit real-world applicability.

The rejection-sampling procedure for postfix completion may become expensive for arbitrary masks; Table 3 reports average trials, but worst-case complexity and failure modes are not fully characterized.

The technical novelty is incremental relative to randomized-permutation AR (RandAR) and order-annealing AR (RAR); the main contribution is the spanning-tree sampling and BFS traversal rather than a new architecture, tokenizer, or training objective.

The empirical scope is restricted to ImageNet class-conditional generation at 256x256; larger-scale, text-to-image, and multimodal AR settings are not explored, so the broader impact on general visual generation remains to be demonstrated.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized. The central idea (using the BFS traversal order of a uniform spanning tree sampled on the patch lattice as the AR sequence order) is simple and easy to follow, and Figure 2 communicates both the training/inference pipeline and the postfix-completion procedure effectively.

The controlled ablation in Table 2 is the strongest part of the paper: under identical model configurations, training with spanning-tree orders substantially outperforms training with random permutations (FID 2.24 vs 3.57), and random-permutation training cannot be rescued by spanning-tree inference. This isolates the effect of the proposed order reasonably well.

The inference-time construction for postfix completion is concretely specified (Algorithm 1) and accompanied by a quantitative study of rejection-sampling efficiency (Table 3), showing BFS with a farthest-root heuristic requires ~1.15-5.59 trials versus 13-89 for DFS. This is a useful practical contribution.

The scaling study up to 1.5B parameters (STAR-B/L/XL/XXL) is reasonably thorough, and the entropy analyses (Figures 3, 4, and Figure A in the supplement) provide a plausible, if descriptive, link between the design and the center-bias/locality priors of image tokens.

The method enables a capability (arbitrary-order postfix completion / inpainting) that a fixed raster-scan AR model cannot support at inference, which is a genuine, if modest, advantage over the RAR baseline.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are marginal and mixed. On ImageNet 256 class-conditional generation, STAR-XXL (FID 1.55, IS 338.8) is slightly worse on FID than the RAR-XXL baseline it builds upon (1.48/326.0), and it does not surpass MAR-H or VAR-d30 on FID. The claim that STAR 'maintains sampling performance' is only weakly supported: in the controlled Table 2 comparison, spanning-tree training yields FID 2.24 versus 2.04 for raster-scan, i.e., a worse FID (though a better IS).

The paper does not isolate why spanning trees specifically are beneficial. There is no comparison to other structured orders that also encode locality/center-bias (e.g., Hilbert or Morton curves, diagonal orders, snake orders with varying starts, or randomized raster-scan variants). Without such baselines, the specific contribution of the spanning-tree construction over 'any locality-respecting order' remains unestablished.

The theoretical motivation is weak. The argument that the spanning-tree sample space is 'distinctly smaller' than the N! permutation space is not a rigorous justification for improved sampling performance, and the authors themselves fall back on empirical results. The number-of-spanning-trees asymptotic (exp(N z_G), z_G ~ 1.166) is a size argument, not a performance argument.

The inpainting evaluation is limited and arguably unfair: only RAR is compared, and RAR is evaluated via teacher forcing without sampling, which the authors acknowledge. Reported inpainting FIDs are very high (~2.4) and no comparison is made to masked-token models (e.g., MaskGIT, MAR) that natively support inpainting, so the claimed flexibility advantage is not convincingly quantified.

The 'minimal changes to the conventional AR architecture' claim is overstated: the method inherits RAR-style order annealing, adaLN class conditioning, and the additional next-token positional embeddings from RandAR/RAR, so the architectural footprint is not trivially small.
Limitations are not discussed, and the framing of STAR as 'a new building block for future work' overstates the maturity and generality of what is essentially a change to the sequence-order prior.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated structured sequence-order randomization for autoregressive visual generation using BFS traversal of uniform spanning trees rooted at random corners.
Clear theoretical connection to permutation AR modeling and masked token prediction, with an intuitive analysis of locality and center bias via conditional entropy measurements.
Extensive experiments on ImageNet 256x256 across four model scales, multiple baselines (RAR, RandAR, DiT, VAR, MAR, LlamaGen), and ablations on traversal, root selection, and masking strategies.
Strong image inpainting results compared with RAR, RandAR, and DiT, demonstrating region-level modification capability with minimal changes to the Decoder-only Transformer architecture.
Good reproducibility: code is available, and hyperparameters, masking strategy, and implementation details are provided in the supplementary material.
The method incurs negligible inference overhead and includes a quantitative efficiency analysis of BFS vs DFS rejection sampling for postfix completion.
weaknesses: Generation performance is not state-of-the-art and underperforms RAR on FID; the claim of 'maintaining generation performance' should be qualified as a trade-off, especially since raster-scan has better FID in the controlled ablation (Table 3).

Image inpainting evaluation relies mainly on FID/IS and lacks per-image reconstruction metrics (e.g., PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), making it difficult to assess whether partial observations are faithfully respected.

The masking assumption (mask does not cover all corners and does not disconnect partial observations) is restrictive; arbitrary masks require multi-turn inference, which is discussed only in the supplementary material.

Comparison with RAR/DiT for inpainting may be affected by different conditioning and inference protocols (teacher forcing, latent blending), so the reported advantage may be partially protocol-dependent.
Theoretical arguments for why uniform spanning tree orders improve convergence are largely empirical and conjectural; no formal convergence guarantee or finite-sample analysis is provided.
Training overhead of UST sampling is not reported, despite claims of no increased training complexity; only inference overhead is measured.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: replacing the dichotomy between fixed raster-scan order and unstructured random permutation with a structured subset of permutations (BFS traversal of uniform spanning trees) that preserves image priors such as center bias and locality while retaining enough flexibility for editing. The framing via Figure 1 is clear and the connection to prior knowledge is insightful.

The paper provides a principled justification for why random permutation degrades convergence and why the spanning-tree subset retains the advantages of raster-scan order, supported by an entropy analysis of conditional model entropy versus token position and Manhattan distance (Figure 3), and by the fact that the number of spanning trees grows as exp(N z_G), far smaller than N!.

Strong, adequately-supported experimental results. STAR outperforms RandAR consistently in both generation and inpainting (Table 1, Table 2) and is competitive with state-of-the-art models (RAR, VAR, LlamaGen) without requiring order-annealing or architectural changes. The native inpainting comparison is particularly convincing, with STAR substantially beating RAR and DiT across all masking ratios (Table 2, Figure 6, Figure 7).

The technical construction of the BFS traversal for postfix completion is carefully developed. Algorithm 1, the depth condition in Eq. 5, and the choice of the farthest corner as root (with rejection sampling) are thoughtful, and Table 4 convincingly demonstrates the superiority of BFS over DFS in terms of trials and failure rate.

Ablations are comprehensive and address the right questions: the source of advantage (locality vs. center bias), comparison against permutation and annealing strategies (Table 3), entropy uniformity across token positions (Figure 8b), and computational overhead (negligible at 0.56 ms per instance).

Good reproducibility practices: code is released, supplementary provides detailed hyperparameters (Table A), training cost in GPU days, and a precise random masking strategy (Algorithm A). The architectural changes relative to the standard decoder-only Transformer are minimal, which is a genuine practical strength.

The authors honestly discuss limitations, including the masking assumption violated in realistic scenarios (supplementary Section A) and propose a multi-turn decomposition workaround, which strengthens the scientific case.
weaknesses: The overall contribution is an incremental but clever improvement over random-permutation AR (RandAR), and the theoretical analysis is largely empirical/conjectural (the paper explicitly calls the entropy analysis a conjecture). The claimed 'prior knowledge' benefit of spanning trees is supported by correlation rather than rigorous derivation, so the causal story behind why spanning trees converge faster than random permutation remains somewhat intuitive rather than proven.

Evaluation is confined to class-conditional ImageNet-1k at 256x256. Text-to-image, higher-resolution, and larger-scale settings (where the trade-offs might differ) are not explored, limiting the demonstrated generality. Given the paper positions STAR as a building block for early-fusion multimodal models, evidence on a multimodal setting would substantially strengthen the claims.

The masking assumption (mask must not cover all corners and must not disconnect the partial observation) is a real restriction; the single-turn inpainting claim therefore holds only for a subset of realistic masks. The multi-turn workaround in the supplementary is reasonable but is not evaluated quantitatively, leaving an important practical gap.

The tie-breaking rule for BFS is fixed and acknowledged as not widely explored; since BFS ordering is central to both training and inference, the sensitivity of results to this choice is not fully analyzed.

Some baseline comparisons could be more balanced. RAR uses an annealing strategy requiring extra hyperparameters, but the paper does not fully isolate how much of STAR's advantage over RAR in inpainting is due to native sequence-order flexibility versus other training details. The generation FID gap between STAR-XXL (1.55) and RAR-XXL (1.48) is small and within noise, so the headline generation claim should be stated more cautiously.

The representation-learning experiment (Figure 9, Section 5) is interesting but thin and somewhat disconnected from the main contribution; it is based on CIFAR-100 and does not deeply validate the claimed benefit.

strengths: The core idea—using the BFS traversal of a uniformly sampled spanning tree (rooted at a random corner) as a structured sequence-order randomization strategy—is genuinely novel and elegantly motivated. It is a principled middle ground between fixed raster-scan order and unconstrained random permutation, and it is grounded in prior knowledge (center bias, locality) rather than being an ad-hoc heuristic.

The method requires only minimal changes to a standard decoder-only Transformer (extra next-token positional conditioning, same as permutation AR), which preserves the architectural simplicity and compatibility with early-fusion multimodal models that the authors emphasize.

The BFS-based postfix-completion argument (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1, Eq. 5) is well-reasoned and correctly identifies why BFS is preferable to DFS for rejection sampling; the accompanying efficiency analysis in Table 4 (trial counts and failure rates across masking ratios) is a concrete and useful validation.

The ablation and analysis sections are unusually thorough for this class of paper: the entropy-vs-distance analysis (Fig. 3b), the center-bias quartile analysis (Fig. 8a), the conditional-entropy comparison across orderings (Fig. 8b), and the representation-learning probe (Fig. 9) all add interpretive value beyond headline numbers.

Empirically, STAR clearly and consistently outperforms the most directly relevant baseline, RandAR (random permutation), on both generation and inpainting (Tables 1–2), supporting the central claim that structure-preserving randomization is better than unstructured randomization.
weaknesses: The headline claim that STAR 'preserves sampling performance' is only weakly supported. Against the strongest and most comparable raster-scan AR baseline (RAR), STAR is consistently worse on pure generation (e.g., STAR-XL 1.65 vs RAR-XL 1.50 FID; STAR-XXL 1.55 vs RAR-XXL 1.48), and STAR-B 2.24 vs RAR-B 1.95. The paper frames this as 'sufficiently comparable,' but the generation advantage is effectively deferred entirely to the inpainting task, so the paper is really an inpainting paper, not a general 'generation + editing' paper as claimed.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only class-conditional ImageNet-1k at 256×256. There is no text-to-image, no larger-scale or higher-resolution setting, and no comparison at the multi-billion-parameter scale where AR models are actually competitive (e.g., LlamaGen-3B is listed but not directly comparable). The generality of the method is therefore not established.

The inpainting evaluation rests on restrictive assumptions on the mask M (does not cover all corners; does not disconnect the partial observation). These assumptions are precisely what makes the postfix-completion construction tractable, and the paper defers violations to the supplementary (multi-turn decomposition). Since arbitrary editing masks routinely violate these conditions, the practical scope of the claimed editing capability is smaller than the framing suggests, and the randomly-connected mask generator (Algorithm A) is essentially designed to satisfy the method's own assumptions, which risks a self-favorable evaluation protocol.

The theoretical justification is largely conjectural. The paper itself says the design 'stems from the conjecture' about prior knowledge, and the entropy-equivalence claim is acknowledged not to hold empirically. The explanation for why spanning trees help (uniform prediction difficulty) is speculation without a formal argument or controlled test isolating the cause.

Baselines are unevenly matched: the raster-scan AR numbers come from LlamaGen with different tokenizers/parameter counts, and RAR additionally uses an annealing schedule and a different training recipe, so attributing gains to the sequence-order strategy alone is difficult. The cleanest comparison (vs RandAR) is against a relatively weak baseline.

Minor but non-trivial presentation issues: the footnote promising code is left as an empty link, and the causal mechanism linking sequence-order structure to convergence speed remains an intuition rather than a demonstrated result.
